title: ArrayPool<T> and MemoryPool<T>
description: Use ArrayPool<T> and MemoryPool<T> to reduce allocation pressure, understand pooling strategies, and avoid common pitfalls.

data.text: In high-performance .NET code, the same array size is often allocated and discarded repeatedly. A web API that processes JSON requests might allocate 4 KB byte arrays for every request. A file processing service might allocate 256 KB buffers for every file. The garbage collector eventually reclaims these arrays, but the constant churn puts pressure on the LOH and increases pause times. `ArrayPool<T>` and `MemoryPool<T>` solve this by renting buffers from a shared pool instead of allocating new ones every time.

Array pooling is not free. The pool must manage concurrent access, decide when to keep or trim buffers, and handle buffer return races. But the cost of pooling is far lower than the cost of repeatedly allocating and collecting large arrays. The .NET runtime itself uses array pools internally for operations like `String.Create`, `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes`, and the HTTP request body pipeline. Using these pools in your own code gives you the same benefit.

`ArrayPool<T>` is a simple abstraction with two methods: ` Rent(int minimumLength)` returns an array that is at least as large as the requested length, and `Return(T[] array, bool clearArray)` returns the array to the pool. The pool may return an array larger than you requested — it reuses arrays from its free list and does not slice them. When you rent an array, treat it as read-write but respect its actual `Length`. Always return arrays when you are done; failing to return an array causes the pool to allocate a replacement, defeating the purpose.

data.title: Using ArrayPool<T> correctly

data.text: `MemoryPool<T>` returns `IMemoryOwner<T>` instances that wrap a pooled `Memory<T>`. The key difference from `ArrayPool<T>` is ownership semantics: `IMemoryOwner<T>` implements `IDisposable`, and disposing it returns the memory to the pool. This makes `MemoryPool<T>` ideal for scenarios where you need a `Memory<T>` or `IMemoryOwner<T>` — such as pipelines that process data in chunks, or custom `IBufferWriter<T>` implementations.

data.title: Using MemoryPool<T> with IMemoryOwner

data.text: The default `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` instance has a maximum array length of 2,097,152 bytes (2 MB) and a maximum retained array count per length bucket. When you rent an array larger than 2 MB, the pool creates a new array without pooling it. You can create a custom `ArrayPool<T>` with `ArrayPool.Create<T>(int maxArrayLength, int maxArraysPerBucket)` to adjust these limits for your workload. For example, if your application routinely processes 10 MB buffers, configure a pool with a higher `maxArrayLength`.

data.title: Creating a custom ArrayPool configuration

items: **Forgetting to return** — always return pooled arrays in a `finally` block or use `using` with `IMemoryOwner<T>`.
**Rented array is larger than requested** — the pool returns the nearest power-of-two size. Always use `AsSpan(0, actualLength)`.
**Data leakage** — pooled arrays retain old data. Call `Return(array, clearArray: true)` if the next consumer should not see previous contents.
**Pinning pooled arrays long-term** — pinning a pooled array for extended periods fragments the LOH. Release the pin as soon as possible.
**Using after return** — once returned, the array belongs to the pool. Do not read or write it after returning.

data.title: Use System.IO.Pipelines for I/O-heavy code
data.text: If you are processing network streams or files, consider `System.IO.Pipelines` instead of manually renting arrays. Pipelines use `ArrayPool<byte>` internally and provide a `PipeReader` and `PipeWriter` that handle buffer management, backpressure, and chunk boundaries. The result is less code, fewer bugs, and the same allocation reduction.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared` rents byte arrays without heap allocation, reducing GC pressure for repeated buffer usage.
`MemoryPool<T>` returns `IMemoryOwner<T>` for owned `Memory<T>` that is returned to the pool on dispose.
Always return rented arrays in a `finally` block; never use an array after returning it to the pool.
Configure custom pool limits when working with buffers larger than 2 MB or with high concurrency.
